items.title: Takeaways on Jaylen Brown's introductory Sixers press conference
items.content:
Takeaways on Jaylen Brown's introductory Sixers press conference  originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

A little over a month since the Sixers shook up the NBA summer by trading for him, Jaylen Brown held his first press conference in Philadelphia.

Here’s what stood out from Brown’s introductory press conference Thursday:

The shock factor How did Brown initially react to the news of the trade? 

“When I first (learned) I got traded, I just threw my phone across the room,” he said with a laugh.

Multiple Sixers soon reached out to Brown and welcomed him aboard, including Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe and Joel Embiid. Still, on a day that included posing for photos with his No. 7 Sixers jersey and throwing out the first pitch at the Phillies game, Brown acknowledged his new reality hasn’t entirely sunk in yet. 

Jaylen Brown, the Sixers’ new No. 7: pic.twitter.com/XA0Wzlr6uk

— Noah Levick (@NoahLevick) August 6, 2026

First pitch duties for the newest Sixer 🫡 pic.twitter.com/AyKkjQ59bU

— NBC Sports Philadelphia (@NBCSPhilly) August 6, 2026

“There’s been a lot of emotions,” he said. “It’s been a process. To be honest, I’m still processing to some degree. One, the excitement of coming to a new city, new place, new expectations, new energy. And then also leaving somewhere that you’ve been for a very, very long time. 

“I’ve been in Boston for 10 years. I’m 29 years old, so I was there a third of my life. I met some lifelong friends, some people that I’ll still be connected to. … It’s just a process. Just like everybody else has to deal with certain things, it’s no different. It’s just been public; that’s the only difference.”

Focused on winning and work Brown was crystal clear about his priorities. 

Details will matter for the Sixers’ dramatically revamped roster, but the five-time All-Star wing’s drive to win is simple. 

“I’m not sure completely yet,” Brown said when asked where he envisions himself most helping the Sixers. “I think we’ll figure it out as time goes on. … But I’m excited to just be myself. That’s one thing I can promise the city, the organization and the coaching staff, that I’m going to come in every single day and be myself. Put my best foot forward, lead with my integrity, lead with my mentality and lead with my capacity and my will to win. 

“So we’ll figure out the X’s and O’s, the ins and outs, but winning is the agenda. That’s the first thing that’s on my mind.” 

Brown’s new teammates certainly won’t be strangers at training camp.

“We talk damn near every day almost,” he said. “We’ve got group chats, multiple now, and we’re all trying to figure this thing out. LeBron (James), he’s active in the group chat. We’re just all trying to get on the same page. I think everybody knows how incredible the opportunity that we have is, but we’ve also got to put in the work. My focus is on that — putting in the work, earning the respect from the city, from the coaching staff.

items.title: The Spurs need Luke Kornet to develop a floater to be a playoff contributor

Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images	The Spurs’ bench was largely a disappointment in the playoffs after being a huge strength in the regular season. While Sixth Man of the Year Keldon Johnson will rightfully get the most scrutiny for his struggles on offense, Luke Kornet had his own issues not only on defense but also scoring inside against better interior defenses.

Kornet is largely a finished product by now, so expecting him to alter his offensive game severely to account for his athletic limitations is too optimistic. That said, there is one relatively simple weapon to develop that he could add to his arsenal, which could make a huge impact on his viability as a playoff scorer and overall offensive player: a floater.

Kornet’s shot profile seemed optimized, at least for the regular season, based on his skills. He gave up on the three-pointer he tried to develop earlier in his career and only takes shots close to the basket now that are largely created for him. He sets screens and dives or roams the dunker spot. Of his 330 field goal attempts, 291 came in the restricted area, and by being close to the rim, he maximized his valuable offensive rebounding. At age 31, Kornet found success as an inside scorer, and he plays to his strengths.

The problem he ran into in the postseason was better rim protection that neutralized his inside scoring, which was his only weapon. On the surface, Kornet going from shooting 65.9 percent in the restricted area to 61.2 percent doesn’t seem like that big of an issue, but since scoring close to the rim is the only way he can get buckets, it was damaging for a second unit that often struggled to create good looks,

Now, with Kornet, his value was always expected to mostly be derived from his defense, so it’s tempting to dismiss any complaints about his scoring. Still, we can’t ignore that San Antonio scored over 10 fewer points per 100 possessions when he played. There’s a strong case to be made that his individual struggles were more a symptom of poor perimeter shot creation than anything else, while the on/off numbers are a reflection of Victor Wembanyama’s greatness, but the fact remains: the Spurs were slightly worse than their average on defense with Kornet playing and absolutely horrendous on offense in the playoffs.
